rows.title: How a $175 COVID-19 test led to $2,479 in charges
rows.standfirst: A global pandemic ravaging America is no time to forget the first rule of American health care: There is no set price. One out-of-network medical provider in Texas seeks permission from patients to charge fees as high as six figures to their insurance.

rows.title: Texas lifts tampon ban at bar exam after complaints over discriminatory policy
rows.standfirst: The state’s board of law examiners said in late July that test takers will be allowed to bring feminine hygiene products in clear plastic bags with them to the grueling, multiday exam that’s needed to obtain a law license.

rows.title: Gov. Greg Abbott will skip Republican National Convention to deal with coronavirus
rows.standfirst: Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick will instead chair the Texas delegation to the pared-down convention later this month in North Carolina.

rows.title: Austin protesters clash with police in the wake of Garrett Foster’s death
rows.standfirst: Saturday marked another night of demonstrations against police brutality in Austin, but tensions were heightened because of last week’s shooting death of Garrett Foster, a 28-year-old protester, by a man who has not been charged.

rows.title: Despite promising to step aside after racist Facebook post, Keith Nielsen becomes Harris County GOP chair
rows.standfirst: Nielsen said earlier this summer that he would forfeit the job amid condemnation for sharing a graphic on Facebook that juxtaposed a Martin Luther King Jr. quote with a banana.

rows.title: Analysis: August agenda for local government includes schools, police spending, property taxes and a pandemic
rows.standfirst: Local governments in Texas finish their spending plans and set their tax rates in August, an annual exercise that includes some hot topics in this pandemic year, like police spending, public schools and property taxes.

rows.title: Joe Biden’s campaign names first Texas hires for general election
rows.standfirst: The announcement comes as polls continue to show a close race in Texas between the presumptive Democratic nominee and President Donald Trump.

rows.title: El Pasoans remember victims of the Walmart shooting one year later
rows.standfirst: A year after the mass shooting in El Paso, where 23 people were killed at a Walmart in what was the worst attack on Latinos in modern U.S. history, we sent Tribune photographers to document a city still in mourning.

rows.title: Texas sales tax collections went up in July — and were higher than one year ago
rows.standfirst: Texas collected $2.98 billion in sales tax revenue in July — 4.3% more than in July 2019. Comptroller Glenn Hegar said the number was “better than expected.”

rows.title: “Forgiveness isn’t given lightly”: El Pasoans balance healing with anger a year after Walmart massacre
rows.standfirst: An undercurrent of fear and anger remains in the Texas city one year after a gunman confessed to targeting Hispanic people in one of the state’s deadliest mass shootings.

rows.title: Federal agents are expelling asylum seekers as young as 8 months from the border, citing COVID-19 risks
rows.standfirst: Thousands of migrant children have been expelled by the Trump administration since March. Some have been held in hotels without access to lawyers or family. Advocates say many are now “virtually impossible” to find.

rows.title: Why Texas’ coronavirus data comes with caveats
rows.standfirst: It’s hard to collect good numbers on an unknown virus, and Texas health officials have made errors. But experts say the state’s coronavirus data is useful as long as users understand its limitations.

rows.title: Gov. Greg Abbott stresses local school officials “know best” whether schools should reopen
rows.standfirst: Abbott said the state will provide schools with personal protective equipment to prepare for the new year.

rows.title: National Democrats commit at least $1 million to MJ Hegar’s effort to unseat U.S. Sen. John Cornyn
rows.standfirst: The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee announced it “will make a seven-figure coordinated investment for the general election in Texas.” It’s the first time it has made such an investment in a Texas race.

rows.title: Watch Gov. Greg Abbott address the need for more hospital beds in the Rio Grande Valley at 2:45 p.m.
rows.standfirst: The governor will be speaking at the McAllen Convention Center, which was recently converted into a hospital to help meet the region’s needs during the coronavirus pandemic.

rows.title: An abrupt change to the census deadline shortened the response period by a month, increasing fears of an undercount in Texas
rows.standfirst: The Census Bureau on Monday lopped a month off the time people have to respond to the 2020 count. Texas is already lagging behind the country in response rates, with low-income and Hispanic Texans at high risk of being missed.

rows.title: Analysis: The Texas Legislature can meet for up to 140 days. The pandemic raises a question: Should it?
rows.standfirst: The Legislature starts its next regular session in January and can meet for up to 140 days. That gives lawmakers time to consider more than 6,000 bills. During a pandemic, they might want to do a lot less.

rows.title: Private schools in Texas limit enrollment as they aim to reopen classrooms
rows.standfirst: Dependent on tuition money, private schools are eager to get children back into their classrooms. But they know inadequate safety measures could make them vulnerable to lawsuits.

rows.title: Lessons from the Field
rows.standfirst: Corporate leaders from H-E-B, Walmart, and KPMG talk about navigating the COVID-19 crisis and responding to rocky economic times. Watch video series here.

rows.title: Five lawmakers sue Gov. Greg Abbott over $295 million contact tracing deal
rows.standfirst: “The Texas Constitution requires a separation of powers, and that separation leaves policy-making decisions with the Texas Legislature,” argues a lawsuit from five of the Legislature’s most conservative members.

rows.title: TribCast: Reading the political tea leaves on Biden in Texas and a census undercount
rows.standfirst: On this week’s TribCast, Alexa talks to Matthew, Patrick and Cassi about the Biden campaign’s recent activity in Texas, the fallout of a census undercount and early indications of what the legislative session might look like in a pandemic.

rows.title: Inside the Trump campaign’s effort — and struggle — to win over Black voters in Texas
rows.standfirst: The Trump campaign has held events across the country to chip away at his broad unpopularity with Black voters and flip the narrative that he is hostile to people of color.

rows.title: T-Squared: Welcoming our first-ever RevLab cohort
rows.standfirst: Revenue Lab, the Tribune’s in-house research and training center, is hosting 14 publishers from around the country for a focused, 8-week program on the subject of creating and hosting successful events

rows.title: UT-Austin will test 5,000 people a week for coronavirus and cover out-of-pocket costs for students
rows.standfirst: The university plans to test all of its campus residence hall students by the beginning of September. It will continue to identify individuals or groups on campus strategically to test those at a higher risk of disease spread and perform random testing.

rows.title: UT planning to limit stadium capacity to 25%. Here’s what you need to know about Texas college football during the pandemic.
rows.standfirst: Texas schools in the Big 12 and SEC are still planning to play this fall.

rows.title: Texas to allow limited visitation in nursing homes with no active coronavirus cases
rows.standfirst: Nursing homes remain hot spots for the virus, with 57% still reporting active cases. Limited visits will be allowed both indoors and outdoors at facilities where there are no cases among residents or staff.

rows.title: Texas was always key to Democrats’ 2020 congressional ambitions. Less than three months from Election Day, their confidence is growing.
rows.standfirst: With nine races on the national radar, the congressional battlefield in Texas is expansive.

rows.title: Analysis: Opening Texas schools is 2020’s top election issue
rows.standfirst: During a pandemic, an economic recession and public protests against racial injustice and police violence, it’s hard to say what Texas voters will be thinking about in this year’s election. Here’s a candidate: Reopening schools.

rows.title: With school reopening, Gov. Greg Abbott sets off another debate over whether local or state officials are in control
rows.standfirst: Abbott’s decision to curb the role of local health authorities in school reopening decisions has added to the ongoing conflict between him and local governments during the pandemic, with mayors and judges voicing frustration over having their hands tied by the state’s response.

rows.title: The only Texas prison reporting zero coronavirus cases is where inmates make soap. But that’s not what’s credited with protecting it.
rows.standfirst: Of more than 100 Texas prison units, the Roach Unit’s apparent ability to avoid the virus has been attributed to a remote location and a warden who strictly enforces precautionary measures.

rows.title: Texas universities have started shedding jobs and are bracing for a serious financial hit
rows.standfirst: It’s impossible to foretell the coronavirus pandemic’s full financial impact on state universities, public and private, but some have already faced millions in lost revenue and unexpected costs. Things will only get worse.

rows.title: Super PAC launches to help Joe Biden win Texas
rows.standfirst: The group, Blue Texas PAC, comes as it remains to be seen how much the Biden campaign will invest in Texas. Polls are showing a close race here.

rows.title: Texas Dove Hunting With Guns.com
rows.standfirst: Want to get out in the field and take advantage of the Lone Star State’s renowned dove season, but find yourself falling short in the gear department? The solution to that is just a click away.

rows.title: Coronavirus outbreak at Houston-area nursing home kills 17 residents
rows.standfirst: The news comes as Texas resumes limited visitations in nursing homes and assisted-living facilities that meet certain requirements.

rows.title: Local GOP officials poised to select Texas’ newest member of Congress, replacing John Ratcliffe in atypical election
rows.standfirst: Ratcliffe was confirmed earlier this summer as director of national intelligence, paving the way for party officials in his deep-red district to replace him on the November ballot.

rows.title: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton wants judge recused from his criminal case, promising further delays in years-old prosecution
rows.standfirst: Paxton was indicted for felony securities fraud in July 2015 but has yet to go to trial as attorneys duke out side battles over venue and prosecutor pay.

rows.title: Texas A&M can’t remove Sul Ross statue without the Legislature’s approval, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton says
rows.standfirst: Without approval from the Texas Legislature, Texas A&M University leaders cannot remove the Lawrence Sullivan Ross statue on campus, Paxton said Friday. If they decide to relocate it, it must be in a “prominent” location, he added.

rows.title: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton says local governments can’t stop or delay evictions
rows.standfirst: The nonbinding opinion comes as housing experts and advocates fear that the COVID-19 recession will prompt a surge in evictions across the state.

rows.title: Out of work and behind on rent, this mom says the pandemic is taking a toll on her mental health
rows.standfirst: The South Texas woman says that since losing her job in late May, her anxiety and depression have made it “very difficult to try and keep it together.” Listen to her story in the weekend edition of The Brief podcast.

rows.title: Texas State Sen. Pat Fallon wins GOP nomination to replace John Ratcliffe on November ballot, becoming Ratcliffe’s likely successor
rows.standfirst: Fallon moves on to a November challenge with a Democratic opponent in the solidly red district. The vacancy was created when Ratcliffe was confirmed as U.S. director of national intelligence.

rows.title: Analysis: The opening line in every Texas political debate
rows.standfirst: School openings, government hearings, going to bars, voting, shopping, even the doings at the Texas Capitol hinge on the same issues: whether it’s safe to gather, and how to go about it.

rows.title: Restaurants, bars and breweries scramble to reinvent themselves to get around Gov. Greg Abbott’s bar shutdown
rows.standfirst: Businesses that make up most of their sales with alcohol were closed down by Abbott’s latest shutdown order, leaving them to maneuver through loopholes to reopen.

rows.title: ICE is making sure migrant kids don’t have COVID-19, then expelling them to “prevent the spread” of COVID-19
rows.standfirst: The administration has used infection risk to justify expelling thousands of children without legal protections. But it’s only expelling kids who’ve tested negative.

rows.title: Coronavirus testing in Texas plummets as schools prepare to reopen
rows.standfirst: Texas’ low number of tests and large percentage of positive results suggest inadequacies in the state’s public health surveillance effort at a time when school reopenings are certain to increase viral spread, health experts said.

rows.title: Local health authority resigns in Texas border county battered by coronavirus
rows.standfirst: Dr. Jose Vazquez resigned from his position as health authority after members of the commissioners court rejected increasing his pay from $500 a month to $10,000.

rows.title: $400 in extra unemployment benefits remain uncertain in Texas after Trump’s executive order
rows.standfirst: The order could face legal challenges, and Texas might have to chip in a quarter of the cost. State leaders have not said how they’ll respond.

rows.title: What losing football to COVID-19 would mean for Texas college towns: “It’s like losing Christmas”
rows.standfirst: Economists said canceling football would be devastating to local businesses that rely on the huge influxes of cash from home games. Meanwhile, athletics officials weigh whether they can risk the health and welfare of student athletes.

rows.title: T-Squared: Okay, *this* is the best Texas Tribune Festival program ever
rows.standfirst: 250 speakers. 100 sessions. 30 thought-provoking days. And you don’t have to leave your comfiest chair.

rows.title: Gov. Greg Abbott says Texans must be vigilant to slow the spread of coronavirus
rows.standfirst: At a pair of press conferences on Tuesday, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott expressed optimism about the recent decline of hospitalizations. Still: He warned Texans to stay cautious.

rows.title: White House acknowledges new unemployment assistance less than what President Trump originally touted
rows.standfirst: Under President Donald Trump’s directive, the federal government may only have enough money to pay the enhanced $300 weekly benefits for about five weeks. The extra federal benefit was previously $600 a week.

rows.title: In a first for major leagues since pandemic, FC Dallas soccer team to play in front of thousands of fans
rows.standfirst: A maximum of 5,110 fans will be in attendance for the game Wednesday, which is happening as other major league sports continue to play in empty arenas.

rows.title: Analysis: The election won’t humble the coronavirus. It’s the other way around.
rows.standfirst: When general election voting starts in two months, Texas voters will know some things they don’t know today to help them make decisions, like what actually happens when you open public schools or allow college football to proceed.

rows.title: Trump called the USMCA the best trade deal ever. Analysts say it’s not likely to help Texas during the pandemic.
rows.standfirst: The COVID-19 pandemic has clobbered the Texas economy and trade with Mexico, clouding the trade deal’s potential impacts, experts say.

rows.title: Big 12 OKs football season, paving way for UT-Austin, Texas Tech, TCU and Baylor to play
rows.standfirst: This comes after the Pac-12 and the Big 10 said that they would postpone college football until at least the spring. Southeastern Conference Commissioner Greg Sankey signaled Tuesday that the conference that includes Texas A&M will play this fall.

rows.title: Jay Hartzell named sole finalist for UT-Austin president
rows.standfirst: Hartzell, dean of the University of Texas at Austin’s business school, has served as interim president since April after former president Greg Fenves stepped down after five years at the helm.

rows.title: TribCast: Kamala Harris on the Democratic presidential ticket and the state of college football
rows.standfirst: On this week’s TribCast, Matthew speaks with Ross, Alex and Raga about college football this fall and what Kamala Harris means for Texas Democrats in November.

rows.title: Texas Democrats see a winning formula in Kamala Harris. Will she bring suburban women and Black voters to the polls?
rows.standfirst: State Democrats see her as someone who can excite key voting groups but who won’t alienate more moderate voters.

rows.title: Hope, fear and hula hoops. How four Texas schools are preparing to bring students back into classrooms.
rows.standfirst: Public schools are about to become the next front line in a state struggling to control the coronavirus pandemic. Here’s what it’s like on the ground at four of them.

rows.title: Gov. Greg Abbott says coronavirus hospitalizations, positive cases must decrease before he’ll allow bars to reopen in Texas
rows.standfirst: Abbott also applauded the Big 12 for allowing Texas college football to resume this fall.

rows.title: Austin City Council cuts police department budget by one-third, mainly through reorganizing some duties out from law enforcement oversight
rows.standfirst: Gov. Greg Abbott said Austin officials’ vote “puts the brave men and women of the Austin Police Department and their families at greater risk” — and vowed that the Texas Department of Public Safety will “stand in the gap.”

rows.title: Gov. Greg Abbott says Texas is investigating its high proportion of coronavirus tests coming back positive
rows.standfirst: The governor also said that testing is down statewide possibly because of the closure of some temporary testing sites created in July that targeted various coronavirus hotspots.

rows.title: Texas Legislative Black Caucus unveils the George Floyd Act to ban chokeholds and limit police use of force
rows.standfirst: In a press conference featuring Floyd’s brother, the lawmakers said they hope their bill wins the support of Gov. Greg Abbott.

rows.title: Analysis: Shopping for students without schoolrooms, Texas is spending $250 million to narrow the digital divide
rows.standfirst: In a state where an estimated 30% of the state’s 5.5 million public school students don’t have the right technology for online learning, switching to virtual classrooms is daunting. And expensive.

rows.title: Texas’ largest cities spend more on police than anything else. Activists want more of those funds spent on the social safety net instead.
rows.standfirst: Austin officials slashed their police department’s budget this week as other Texas cities are rethinking how general fund dollars are spent — and whether spending so much to combat crime addresses the poverty that can cause it.

rows.title: The crushing isolation of nursing homes during the pandemic
rows.standfirst: Texas eased restrictions on visitation in long-term care facilities last week, but many families remain unsure if they will be allowed to visit. For those cut off from their loved ones for almost five months, isolation is becoming another very real threat.

rows.title: ICE guards “systematically” sexually assault detainees in an El Paso detention center, lawyers say
rows.standfirst: Allegations include guards attacking victims in camera “blind spots” and telling them that “no one would believe” them in ICE detention centers, which imprison about 50,000 immigrants each year at a taxpayer expense of $2.7 billion.

rows.title: USPS warns Texas that some mail-in ballots may be delayed in November
rows.standfirst: It is unclear how many Texas voters may be affected should delays occur. Texas was among 46 states that received a warning from the United States Postal Service, according to The Washington Post.

rows.title: Advocates urge a legal review of Trump’s immigration policies after report finds two top officials are not eligible to serve
rows.standfirst: A federal report determined that two Department of Homeland Security officials, including the acting secretary, aren’t legally qualified to hold those posts.

rows.title: Texas officials blame coding errors and a system update for recent COVID-19 testing data issues
rows.standfirst: Earlier this week, Texas disclosed more than 124,000 previously unreported COVID-19 tests, at a time when the proportion of positive tests results was drawing attention.

rows.title: Democrats, local election leaders fear Donald Trump’s attacks on mail-in voting foreshadow voter suppression
rows.standfirst: Changes at the U.S. Postal Service have raised concerns about whether ballots will be delivered on time, but local officials and Democrats stress that mail-in voting remains a vital and safe way to cast a ballot.

rows.title: Why voting matters to these Texans — then and now
rows.standfirst: Hear Texas advocates describe their takes on the practice of voting and its importance to themselves and their generation.

rows.title: The Texas Rangers’ lore spurred cultural fawning and sports namesakes that have long masked a history of violence and racism
rows.standfirst: This year’s prevalent and ongoing protests against police brutality have sparked calls for the Rangers’ name to be stricken from the modern-day Texas Department of Public Safety investigative agency, North Texas’ Major League Baseball team and college mascots.

rows.title: When sharing pencils isn’t safe, this San Antonio teacher is helping crowdfund extra school supplies
rows.standfirst: In the weekend edition of The Brief podcast, listen to why Ambra Hernandez felt compelled to launch a Facebook group to help teachers fulfill their longer-than-normal wish lists.

rows.title: Analysis: Voting in Texas is different from other places. It’s a hassle.
rows.standfirst: Lots of states make it as easy as possible to register and vote, whether there’s a pandemic or not. Texas is not one of those states.

rows.title: As the Democratic National Convention begins, some Texas Democrats wish their state had a bigger role
rows.standfirst: Some party leaders have pushed for convention organizers to give more prominent slots to Texans in the convention lineup, eager to show it is a battleground in November.

rows.title: In a pandemic, childhood vaccinations have never been more important
rows.standfirst: As a pediatrician, I know that vaccinations keep our children safe from preventable diseases like the measles. As a parent, I understand the apprehension — or perhaps, fear — some parents have in scheduling office visits during the COVID-19 pandemic to get immunizations and other primary care services for their children.

rows.title: Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick blames the presence of Confederate monuments at the Texas Capitol on Democrats after being urged to remove them
rows.standfirst: Senate Democrats want the symbols taken down, but Patrick said that the party is not committed to a “sincere” or “serious conversation” about the future of the monuments.

rows.title: Texas becomes fourth state to surpass 10,000 COVID-19 deaths
rows.standfirst: New Jersey, New York and California have also exceeded 10,000 known COVID-19 fatalities. Experts say official death tolls are all but certain to be undercounts.

rows.title: What you need to know about Colin Allred and Victoria Neave, two of the DNC’s “rising stars”
rows.standfirst: The Dallas lawmakers are among a group of 17 participating in Tuesday night’s keynote address at the Democratic National Convention.

rows.title: Gov. Greg Abbott, other Texas leaders want to freeze property tax revenues for cities that cut police budgets
rows.standfirst: The state’s three top elected leaders also fiercely criticized the Austin officials who plan to cut up to one-third of their police department’s budget, largely through reorganizing divisions out from under law enforcement.

rows.title: TV ad blitz kicks off in high-profile battle between U.S. Rep. Chip Roy and Wendy Davis
rows.standfirst: Both sides in the race are launching TV ads Tuesday, auguring an expensive, action-packed sprint to November.

rows.title: Harris County joins federal lawsuit trying to extend time for U.S. census count
rows.standfirst: After the Trump administration announced an abrupt change to the census deadline, the largest county in Texas is among those suing to keep the count going until October.

rows.title: Former USPS leader from Texas says Postmaster General Louis DeJoy is “destroying confidence” in the postal service
rows.standfirst: Carolyn Lewis, a former USPS Board of Governors chair, said she has been disturbed by reports of cost-cutting measures and concerns that the mail service will not be able to handle an influx of mailed-in ballots.

rows.title: Texas school district’s dreadlocks ban discriminatory, federal court rules
rows.standfirst: The decision comes a month after the Barbers Hill Independent School District board of trustees voted to keep the dress code policy, which advocates have deemed racist.

rows.title: Sam Houston State University canceled its in-person graduation and fall sports — but hosted a Tiffany Haddish comedy show
rows.standfirst: The school allowed up to 675 students into its indoor Johnson Coliseum to watch comedian Tiffany Haddish on the first day of classes.

rows.title: Analysis: Watch the bottom of Texas ballots for political change — not the top
rows.standfirst: If the decadeslong Republican hold on Texas politics loosens, it might not be at the top of the ticket. Watch the federal and state legislative races, and where the money’s going in those.

rows.title: “We’re being treated as guinea pigs”: Faculty members fear in-person return to Texas universities
rows.standfirst: Some faculty members call the pressure to return to face-to-face instruction a callous decision that prioritizes money and the college experience over the safety of the university community.

rows.title: TribCast: Texas and the DNC, the fight over police funding, and election mailing woes
rows.standfirst: On this week’s Tribcast, Alexa talks to Matthew, Alex and Ross about Texans’ role at the Democratic National Convention, a new front in the local control fight and what election mail concerns could mean for Texas.

rows.title: Jobless Texans still don’t know if they will receive extra unemployment benefits
rows.standfirst: Confusion over unemployment relief in Texas has persisted since President Donald Trump took executive action in early August announcing an extra $400 weekly payment — but only if states administer the funds and chip in a quarter of the cost.

rows.title: Texas Democrats are successfully suing to kick Green Party candidates off the November ballot
rows.standfirst: Democrats won legal rulings Wednesday blocking Green Party nominees for U.S. Senate, railroad commissioner and the 21st Congressional District from appearing on the November ballot.

rows.title: As the Texas restaurant industry struggles, so do farmers, truckers and others in the food supply chain
rows.standfirst: Economic experts say a slow recovery in the industry means problems will persist for the restaurant sector — and businesses in the supply chain on which it relies.

rows.title: In Texas, USPS woes and state deadlines could leave voters without enough time to return mail-in ballots
rows.standfirst: In Texas’ major counties, almost 99% of mail-in ballots were counted during the July primary runoff election, a Tribune analysis shows. But election officials say postal service disarray and a record number of requests mean people should ask for their absentee ballots well before November’s Election Day.

rows.title: Texas will apply for federal program to get extra $300 per week for unemployed Texans
rows.standfirst: At least 10 other states have already applied and been approved for the additional unemployment benefits.

rows.title: Daphne Prairie and other Texas grasslands can store carbon and help fight climate change
rows.standfirst: But there are few pieces of pristine land left like Daphne Prairie, untouched by plow or urban sprawl.

rows.title: UT-Austin students and employees urge officials to stop in-person classes, lower tuition and offer hazard pay
rows.standfirst: The Texas State Employees Union presented a petition that condemns the upcoming return to campus in the midst of the coronavirus pandemic as harmful. Classes start Wednesday.

rows.title: Texas will start posting coronavirus case data from public schools, education commissioner says
rows.standfirst: The data will be posted on a state website and the reporting process will be finalized after input from school superintendents.

rows.title: In shift, Texas begins publishing some data on coronavirus cases at child care centers
rows.standfirst: Without numbers on how many children or staff are in Texas child care facilities — which the state does not report — it’s hard to gauge the magnitude of infections.

rows.title: Nonprofit that financed a private border wall is now the focus of a corruption case
rows.standfirst: Investigators say fundraisers for nonprofit We Build the Wall, including Steve Bannon and founder Brian Kolfage, lied to donors and pocketed funds. Trump has tried to distance himself from the group but Kolfage has bragged about their ties.

rows.title: San Antonio postal union leader describes mass delays, says Postal Service hid backlogged mail from congressman
rows.standfirst: The union leader said tens of thousands of pieces of mail were carted away ahead of U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro’s visit. The office’s delays have been exacerbated by employees missing because of COVID-19 concerns.

rows.title: Analysis: With elections coming, Texas Republican leaders join the thin blue line
rows.standfirst: Freezing local taxes in Texas cities that cut police funding sounds better than it works. But the political angle taken by the state’s top leaders gives them something other than pandemic and recession to talk about this election season.

rows.title: With no end to the shutdown in sight, Texas bar owners and employees are on the brink of losing everything
rows.standfirst: Some bar owners are planning to reopen in defiance of the moratorium, a desperate attempt to generate income — and draw Gov. Greg Abbott’s attention.

rows.title: The Democrats’ national convention shone a spotlight on Texas’ emerging bench — beyond the Castros and O’Rourke
rows.standfirst: During their party’s national convention this week, Democrats got a glimpse of their roster of up-and-coming leaders. Among them were at least four Texans who aren’t the usual suspects.

rows.title: Texas’ July unemployment rate drops slightly to 8%
rows.standfirst: With more than 10,000 Texans dead from COVID-19, economists have warned that until the state gets a handle on the pandemic, the economic recession will not improve.

rows.title: A South Texas chaplain prayed with his hospice patients. Then the coronavirus came for him.
rows.standfirst: The hospital where he had previously ministered to terminally ill patients was full when Adolfo Alvarado Jr. neared death in his Mission home. He was finally admitted, and his daughter watched on her laptop as he died.

rows.title: Texas put hundreds of hours into finding and arresting police brutality protesters. Lawyers call it a “witch hunt.”
rows.standfirst: Two days of unruly protests at the Texas Capitol in May left graffiti on the historic building and cuts and bruises on state police officers. Since then, the Texas Department of Public Safety has spent the summer naming and arresting suspects, the majority of whom are accused of misdemeanors.

rows.title: Out-of-work Texans could start seeing extra $300 in unemployment payments next week
rows.standfirst: On Friday, federal officials gave Texas the green light to provide the additional payments. States can contribute another $100, but Texas does not plan to do so.

rows.title: Here’s how to vote by mail in Texas
rows.standfirst: Your questions answered about who qualifies, when to expect your ballot and how to make sure your vote counts.

rows.title: Two hurricanes could form in the Gulf of Mexico next week, and one storm is heading toward Texas
rows.standfirst: Tropical Depression 14 is forecasted to intensify briefly into a hurricane and then weaken before making landfall early Tuesday. It could hit somewhere near the Texas-Louisiana border.

rows.title: Bucking local health warnings, two private religious schools are set to reopen in hard-hit Rio Grande Valley
rows.standfirst: Desperate to slow the spread of the coronavirus, Cameron County has ordered all schools to keep classrooms closed until late September. But state officials say local health orders don’t apply to private religious schools.

rows.title: The Texas GOP’s new slogan echoes a conspiracy group. Its chair says there’s no connection.
rows.standfirst: The slogan — “We are the storm” — uses language commonly used by QAnon adherents. State GOP Chair Allen West says it’s taken from a favorite quote.

rows.title: Judge won’t be removed from criminal case against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton
rows.standfirst: Paxton’s team had asked that the judge, Jason Luong, be recused from the case because the Texas attorney general’s office is representing him — along with about 20 other Houston-area judges — in an unrelated lawsuit.

rows.title: After recount, Tony Gonzales is still winner of GOP runoff for U.S. Rep. Will Hurd’s seat
rows.standfirst: Gonzales’ runoff opponent, Raul Reyes, announced Friday evening that he was abandoning his recount effort.

rows.title: For this working mom, the risk of her son contracting coronavirus outweighs the need for him to be in class
rows.standfirst: Amy Mason says there are just too many unknowns for her to feel comfortable sending her 4-year-old to school at this point. Listen in the weekend edition of The Brief podcast.

rows.title: Shelley Luther, Dallas salon owner who pressured Texas to reopen salons, says she’s running for state Senate
rows.standfirst: Luther is running to replace state Sen. Pat Fallon, R-Prosper, in a yet-to-be-called special election now that he is poised for a promotion to Congress.

rows.title: U.S. Reps. Will Hurd, Michael McCaul break from Republicans and vote for USPS rescue bill
rows.standfirst: Driven by Democrats worried about mail-in voting being jeopardized this November, members returned to the U.S. Capitol amid summer recess to vote on the legislation.

rows.title: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott declares state of disaster in 23 counties ahead of Hurricane Marco, Tropical Storm Laura
rows.standfirst: With two storms gaining strength in the Gulf of Mexico, Abbott on Sunday declared a state of disaster in coastal counties and warned Texans to remember coronavirus health guidelines.

rows.title: Gov. Greg Abbott sets Sept. 29 special election to replace state Sen. Pat Fallon
rows.standfirst: Minutes after Abbott’s announcement, state Rep. Drew Springer, R-Muenster, announced his campaign for the seat.

rows.title: Analysis: Austin’s police cuts give Texas Republicans new campaign material
rows.standfirst: Texas Republicans who were looking for fertile political ground in the runup to the November elections got a gift from a most unlikely source: the Austin City Council.

rows.title: Texas students said pandemic-era tuition should be cut. But it’s going up at some schools due to distance learning fees.
rows.standfirst: Students grappling with financial upsets and a hurting economy say tuition should be lowered at their Texas universities. But some colleges are adding new fees related to an increase in distance learning.

rows.title: In an investigation tied to private border wall, federal prosecutors have Steve Bannon’s murky nonprofit in their sights
rows.standfirst: Tucked at the bottom of the long indictment against Bannon, prosecutors say they want to seize the assets of his nonprofit Citizens of the American Republic, shedding more light on the secretive political group’s finances.

rows.title: Nearly 350,000 unemployed Texans don’t qualify for extra $300 weekly benefit
rows.standfirst: Texans receiving less than $100 in weekly unemployment benefits do not qualify for the extra $300 weekly payments the Trump administration is distributing to Texas and other states.

rows.title: EPA approves coronavirus cleanser for emergency use in Texas
rows.standfirst: Texas said it would allow American Airlines and two branches of a sports clinic to start using the new product.

rows.title: Texas State University welcomed students back in person Monday. Campus was a ghost town.
rows.standfirst: Monday was the first day of in-person instruction at the San Marcos campus since the coronavirus pandemic raged across Texas, forcing school officials to reinvent the college experience in an attempt to keep students safe.

rows.title: Whether it’s hurricanes or COVID-19, disasters are driving a mental health crisis
rows.standfirst: Mounting catastrophes are sowing stress and trauma. The country’s one program to help reaches only a fraction of survivors.

rows.title: As eviction cases resume in parts of Houston, low-income Texans fear losing a place to live
rows.standfirst: Since Gov. Greg Abbott declared a public health disaster in March, almost one-third of Harris County’s evictions have been filed in the justice of the peace precinct covering the southwestern portion of the county.

rows.title: Several Texas cities issue mandatory evacuation orders as Hurricane Laura strengthens in the Gulf
rows.standfirst: From Galveston to the Louisiana border, Texas communities are telling residents to seek shelter away from the coast as Laura is projected to intensify into a Category 3 hurricane.

rows.title: Texas’ most populous county sending mail-in ballot applications to millions of registered voters
rows.standfirst: Not all of Harris County’s registered voters will ultimately qualify. Texas is among a handful of states with strict eligibility requirements to vote by mail.

rows.title: Analysis: Those aren’t just COVID-19 numbers. They’re Texans.
rows.standfirst: There are 347,700 Texans losing federal supplements to unemployment insurance. And 716,000 students getting laptops and tablets for virtual school. And 11,395 COVID-19 deaths. Each statistic has a human face.

rows.title: In Texas, the lowest-income workers don’t qualify for additional unemployment aid
rows.standfirst: Nearly 350,000 Texans don’t qualify for the extra payment because they either earned too little from the work they lost or didn’t indicate on paperwork that they lost their jobs due to the pandemic.

rows.title: Here’s how education in Texas looks as public schools begin reopening with mostly online classes
rows.standfirst: As schools across the state begin fall instruction, most students will learn from home for at least the first three weeks. That means getting supplies and food to students and finding creative ways to hold their attention.

rows.title: National Democrats add three more Texas congressional districts to target list
rows.standfirst: The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee announced Wednesday it is now targeting Reps. Van Taylor of Plano, Roger Williams of Austin and Ron Wright of Arlington.

rows.title: Dan Crenshaw will make a prime-time appearance at the RNC Wednesday. Here’s what you need to know about the Houston Republican.
rows.standfirst: The U.S. representative is the only Texas elected official to get a prime-time speaking slot.

rows.title: As Hurricane Laura heads for Southeast Texas, officials scramble to evacuate and shelter people during a pandemic
rows.standfirst: The storm is now a Category 4 hurricane whose dangerous winds and storm surge could cause damage along a large swath of the Gulf Coast and Southeast Texas.

rows.title: Experts say disruption to oil and gas industry will depend on Hurricane Laura’s speed
rows.standfirst: Hurricane Laura made landfall just east of the Texas-Louisiana border around midnight Thursday.

rows.title: Still recovering from Harvey, Texans in Beaumont and Port Arthur are now preparing for a new hurricane during the pandemic
rows.standfirst: Groups that have been fixing homes and providing assistance to victims of the 2017 hurricane are now getting ready to face a new disaster, with the added challenge of COVID-19.

rows.title: TribCast: Hurricane Laura, coronavirus on campus and the RNC
rows.standfirst: In this week’s TribCast, Matthew speaks with Ross, Alex and Patrick about the incoming hurricane, the first week of college classes and the Republican National Convention.

rows.title: A Texas teacher who posted Black Lives Matter and LGBTQ posters in her virtual classroom was placed on leave after parents complained
rows.standfirst: School officials said parents complained about the posters. Taylor Lifka was allowed to return Tuesday, but she said she is not prepared to come back until the school commits to more inclusive policies.

rows.title: “It could have been far worse”: Texas and local officials express relief after state avoids massive damage
rows.standfirst: Gov. Greg Abbott said an aerial view of the area revealed more ripped-off rooftops and downed trees in Orange than anywhere else in Texas.

rows.title: Five health experts on the state’s coronavirus data backlog
rows.standfirst: The state disclosed a backlog of more than 850,000 tests this month, which were delayed in part because of coding or formatting errors and a lengthy onboarding process needed to receive reports from laboratories.

rows.title: Hurricane Laura in Texas: President Donald Trump to visit and survey damage
rows.standfirst: We’re tracking the impact of Hurricane Laura, which made landfall after midnight Thursday.

rows.title: Analysis: A weather map for Texas’ COVID-19 response
rows.standfirst: The state has disaster response down to a routine, ready to roll out whenever hurricanes and other bad weather strikes. But that coordination between state and local governments hasn’t been the model for pandemic response.

rows.title: Texas schools must file weekly reports with state on COVID-19 cases
rows.standfirst: Starting Sept. 8, Texas education officials will require all school districts to fill out forms weekly reporting new cases, including whether the infections occurred on or off campus and if the campus closed as a result.

rows.title: Nearly 600,000 Texans will lose access to a program that prevented electricity shut-offs during the pandemic on Oct. 1
rows.standfirst: Once the program ends, customers could be on the hook for partial back payments.

rows.title: Hurricane after hurricane wreaked havoc in Orange, Texas. Finally, residents say they got a break.
rows.standfirst: State and local leaders and thousands of residents surveyed the comparatively little damage with gratitude — and surprise.

rows.title: Special education students lost crucial help when the pandemic hit. Texas schools are still struggling to restore it.
rows.standfirst: Ten percent of Texas public school students need special education resources, and many were left stranded when schools closed abruptly in the spring. Educators and parents face challenges again this fall reconnecting kids with the therapists and specialists they need.

rows.title: Texas Republicans had light presence at national convention amid debate over state’s battleground status
rows.standfirst: Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, who chairs President Donald Trump’s reelection campaign in Texas, said the lack of Texas speakers showed Republicans were not worried about the state.

rows.title: Texas tells Harris County to halt plan to send all voters applications for mail-in ballots
rows.standfirst: The secretary of state’s office threatened legal action against Harris County if it goes ahead with a plan to send applications for mail-in ballots to more than 2 million registered voters.

rows.title: The Texas Senate Hispanic Caucus wants an investigation into Fort Hood. At least nine soldiers stationed there have been found dead this year.
rows.standfirst: The Texas Senate Hispanic Caucus reupped its request on Friday for a congressional investigation into Fort Hood, the Killeen military base.

rows.title: For second time, federal judge finds Texas is violating voter registration law
rows.standfirst: A U.S. district judge found Texas is “legally obligated” to allow voters to simultaneously register to vote with every driver’s license renewal or change-of-address application, and ordered the state to set up a “fully operable” online system by Sept. 23.

rows.title: Four candidates join Shelley Luther, Drew Springer in race to replace state Sen. Pat Fallon
rows.standfirst: Springer, a state representative, and Luther, a Dallas salon owner who was jailed over her refusal to close her business due to the coronavirus pandemic, had previously announced their campaigns.

rows.title: Texas officials want to cut funding for women’s health services while preserving an anti-abortion program
rows.standfirst: An August budget document shows funding for the anti-abortion program would be maintained, but reduced for doctors and clinics that provide reduced-cost contraception and health screenings.

rows.title: “We’re all holding our breath”: Health experts on school reopenings in Texas
rows.standfirst: The Texas Tribune spoke to experts about what the state can expect as schools and universities start school remotely or in person.

rows.title: Analysis: Some Texas voters are still uncertain, but so are the issues
rows.standfirst: Voters who still haven’t decided which candidates to support in November might be uncertain for a good reason: The issues that would help them decide — pandemic, recession and all the rest — are shifting rapidly.

rows.title: This loan company was founded to help Latino immigrants. It has sued thousands of low-income Latinos during the pandemic.
rows.standfirst: A monthslong investigation revealed that Oportun Inc. routinely uses lawsuits to intimidate a vulnerable population into keeping up with high-interest loan payments — even amid COVID-19.

rows.title: Oportun Inc. has filed nearly 10,000 lawsuits this year against lower-income Texans. This is how we found out.
rows.standfirst: Justice of the peace courts, where a majority of debt claims are filed in Texas, aren’t required to report case-level information. Here’s how ProPublica and Texas Tribune reporters got around it to reveal one company’s aggressive tactics.

rows.title: Texas sues Harris County to stop it from sending all voters applications for mail-in ballots
rows.standfirst: The Texas secretary of state had threatened the legal action last week, but Harris County Clerk Chris Hollins indicated he would not drop his effort to send out absentee ballot applications to more than 2 million registered voters.
